description: We are a passionate squad of developers, problem-solvers, and tech enthusiasts brought together for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Combining expertise in software engineering, data analysis, and user experience design, Team Cygnus transforms NASA’s open data into high-impact, interactive digital tools.
summary:
FosholCycle, developed by Team Cygnus, is an interactive crop-sequence explorer that helps farmers and agricultural advisers compare planting options using local crop research and NASA POWER historical weather data.
Starting in Rajshahi, Bangladesh, users select a planting date, first crop, water-access scenario, and comparison priority. Our engine generates dated three-crop sequences and compares completion time, crop-family diversity, temperature match, dry spells, and heavy-rain exposure—while making trade-offs and missing evidence visible.
FosholCycle addresses the “Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data” challenge by connecting Earth observations with agricultural knowledge in an accessible decision-support tool. Rather than prescribing one “best” rotation, it helps users explore possibilities and identify what needs local confirmation.
This matters because a delayed harvest can tighten the next planting window, while variable weather makes planning harder. We are not here to replace farmers’ expertise—we are here to assist, supporting informed choices without claiming guaranteed yields or future weather predictions.
details:
FosholCycle — Smarter Crop Rotations. Resilient Farms.

Developed by Team Cygnus, FosholCycle helps farmers and agricultural advisers explore crop sequences using local agricultural research and NASA historical weather data. Starting in Rajshahi, Bangladesh, we aim to make complex information understandable—not replace farmers’ expertise, but assist it.

What does it do?

Users choose a planting date, first crop, water-access scenario, and comparison priority. Our Python engine, CycleAlgo, checks documented planting windows and duration ranges to generate dated three-crop sequences.

Users can compare completion time, crop-family diversity, temperature match, dry spells, and heavy-rain exposure. The interface shows schedules, trade-offs, sources, and unresolved checks, with up to three sequences displayed side by side.

Benefits and intended impact

One late harvest can tighten the next planting window. FosholCycle helps users understand how crops connect across seasons without processing decades of climate records themselves.

Our goal is to support informed discussions between farmers and advisers. Following local agricultural review, we aim to expand to more districts. The prototype does not yet demonstrate increased yields, income, or soil health.

Tools and technologies

We used Next.js, React, JavaScript/JSX, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet, and Lucide React for the website, and Python for CycleAlgo. NASA POWER API history and cache provide weather evidence; researched CSV crop profiles provide agricultural inputs, exchanged through JSON.

Software checks use Node.js tests, Python unittest, ESLint, and build checks. No custom hardware is required.

What makes it creative?

FosholCycle connects sequence timing, historical weather, and uncertainty in one accessible experience. Instead of producing a single “best rotation” score, it lets users explore priorities while preserving constraints and showing where evidence is missing.

What did we consider?

We prioritized simplicity, accessibility, local relevance, farmer expertise, and responsible interpretation. Weather comparisons use shared complete historical seasons; missing values remain unknown, and ties remain ties.

We distinguish historical exposure from forecasts, gridded observations from field measurements, and crop diversity from measured soil improvement. Map previews are labeled demo data, while planner comparisons use the engine API.

FosholCycle turns complex evidence into clearer choices—keeping farmers and local advisers in control.

Benefits describe the project’s intended value, not measured farm outcomes.
